analytic.title: A Novel Slack-Stealing Scheduling Algorithm for Hard-Real-Time multipleprocessors System

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: When a permanent fault occurs in real-time system with multiple-processors, the slack distribution for different instances of the same task is unfair. The task instance under fault-occurred period (called urgent instance) is usually more urgent than its subsequent ones (called normal instance). In order to resolve the problem, the paper presents a novel slackstealing strategy (referred to as NSS), which delays the execution of normal instance as late as possible. NSS strategy can reserve the slack time for the urgent instance with low priority potentially, thus it has more chance to complete its execution in time. Moreover, we present the corresponding schedulability test and accurate computation of delaying time based on NSS strategy. Extensive simulations reveal that NSS can achieve a remarkable saving on the number of processors required with respect to several well-known fault-tolerant scheduling algorithms.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Hard-real-time systems are widely used in scientific and commercial applications, such as navigation, process control, automated surveillance, and satellite remote sensing, in which periodic critical tasks are required to finish before their deadlines. Moreover, such systems are often deployed in the extreme harsh environments and hardware failures are more than likely in such environments. Therefore, faulttolerance plays an important role in hard-real-time scheduling algorithm. The problem of scheduling of real-time tasks in multiprocessor systems is to determine when and on which processor a given task executes [1,2] and the performance is usually defined as the minimal number of required processors. So, the ultimate goal of the hardreal-time system scheduler is reducing the number of required processors under the premise of guaranteeing schedulability and reliability.

Hard-real-time scheduling is known to be NP-hard, several heuristics to schedule periodic tasks on uniprocessor and multiprocessor systems have been proposed. Rate-Monotonic (RM) algorithm [3] is the optimal fixed-prioritydriven preemptive algorithm for a single processor. In RM algorithm, the task with shortest period has the highest priority. The Completion Time Test (CTT) [4], devised by Joseph and Pandya, is used to check schedulability of a set of fixed-priority tasks on a single processor. RM was generalized to multiprocessor systems by Dhall and Liu and they proposed the Rate-Monotonic First-Fit (RMFF) [5] heuristic, where tasks are considered by RM priority order and assigned to the first processor in which they can be scheduled by RM algorithm.

In terms of fault-tolerance, the Primary-Backup (PB) scheme [6][7][8][9][10] is widely used in hard-real-time distributed systems. In this scheme, each task has at least two copies allocated to different processors: primary copy and backup copy. The status of backup copy can be active or passive: active copy is released simultaneously with its corresponding primary task, while passive copy is released after the failure of its primary task. An active backup has a larger time window for execution than passive backup. However, it makes the duplication waste in the non-fault-occurrence case. In contrast, a passive backup has no such a disadvantage but has tighter timing constraints.

Bertossi et al. combine RMFF with PB and proposed Fault-Tolerant Rate-Moronic First-Fit (FTRMFF) algorithm [11] to tolerate a single permanent fault. FTRMFF algorithm makes full use of the advantages both of passive replication and active replication techniques. However, in FTRMFF, there exists useless execution of active copies, which is the duration after their corresponding primary copies successful finishing. To solve this problem, Bertossi proposed Active Resource Reclaim (ARR) [12] strategy which uses phasing delay [13,14] technique to reduce computation fraction of the active copy that must be executed in the absence of failure of the primary copy. ARR strategy can reduce the overlap between the active task copies and its primary copies and deallocate active task copies as soon as their primary task copies successfully complete. Wang et al. presented TPFTRM algorithm [10], which integrated ARR and taskassignment based on S-Priority [15]. S-Priority strategy intended to assign the tasks whose periods have multiple relationship together, but make the complexity much higher.

The present paper will further improve scheduling performance by borrowing ideas from delaying in the case of failure. Specifically, after a hardware failure occurring, the task instance in current period has the shortest relative deadline and becomes most urgent compared with the subsequent instances. In order to facilitate the description, we define the former as urgent instance and the latter as normal instance. Under the premise of deadline-meeting, we delay the execution of normal instance as late as possible, which can help more instances with lower priority have chance to complete their executions within their urgent periods. We call this as Novel Slack-Stealing (NSS) strategy. In essential, the purpose of NSS strategy is moving the idle slack from normal instance to the urgent instance.

Obviously, NSS strategy is helpful to increase processor utilities and improve scheduling performance compared with ARR. However, it is difficult to implement for the following reasons. First, in ARR, delaying phasing of active backup copy make its every request period is not synchronous with that of its primary copy, which make it is hard to distinguish urgent and normal period for the primary and backup copy of the same task. To solve the problem, we will design a delayer strategy to avoid the asynchronization and implement the same delaying effect of active backup copy as ARR. Second, except for the initial delaying of active backup copy as in ARR, we need consider the delaying of any type tasks after a permanent failure occurring. The last but not the least, our schedulability test needs to accurately calculate the task's Worst Case Response Time (WCRT), the duration from instance's release to completion, in both urgent period and normal period and the calculation of preemptive work time by high priority tasks can not directly adopt the formula in classic LIU model in [3]. The main contribution of the paper is handling these knotty problems. Specifically, we give the determinate calculations of WCRT in urgent period and maximal delay in normal period.

The remaining part of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 gives the notation, the fault-tolerant system assumptions and a formal definition of the scheduling problem. Section 3 deals with the NSS strategy whose implementation includes two computations: the worst case response time in urgent period and maximal delaying in urgent period. Section 4 introduces the extended OneFault schedulability test and the task assignment and recovery in NSS strategy. Section 5 reports extensive simulations where NSS is compared with other classic scheduling algorithms. Finally, conclusions and future work are summarized in Section 6.

The phasing delay technique allows the delay of a passive copy until the completion time of its primary copy so that the passive copy is executed only when the primary task fails. ARR strategy extends phasing delay technique to active backup copy. That is, active backup copy is delayed as late as possible to minimize overlap between this active backup copy and its primary copy in the worst case. Therefore, the unexecuted portion of an active copy can be deallocated as soon as a primary copy has been successfully completed and the processor resource can be used for the execution of another task. For better description, we use the same symbol i dmax to show the maximum phasing delaying of active backup copy i τ . It is noted that, in the worst case, each request period of backup copy 2i τ is at least 2i dmax late than its primary copy 2 1 i τ -. It perhaps causes the following situation: when a permanent fault occurs, the number of request period of primary copy is larger than that of backup copy. To unify urgent and normal period of primary copy and backup copy of the same task, a novel design is present without damaging the effect of phasing delay in ARR strategy. In our scheduling model, each task instance has four states during its lifetime: release, ready, execution and finish. The instance enters its release state at its release time. In the paper, we define a Delayer from Release to Ready (referred to as DRR) for each task, after which its instances become ready state from release state. Only in the ready state, the instance is qualified to compete for processor to schedule by the priority order. The task being processed by processor is called in execution state and completes its execution is called in finish state. Based on the scheduling model, it is easy to achieve ARR strategy by setting primary copy 2 1 i τ -'s DRR to 0 and backup copy 2i τ 's to 2i dmax if it is active or its primary copy's WCRT if passive. The backup copies will be canceled as soon as its primary finishes successfully. DRR is to give the formula definitions of urgent period and normal period for the periodic task. In the worst case, the execution in normal period will not be preempted by the execution of high priority task in its urgent period. Proof. There are three possible cases about the ending of urgent period of low priority task: it is before, equal to or after that of high priority task. For the latter two, when the low priority task enters its normal period, the high priority task has finished its urgent period. It is supposed that when the low priority task enters its normal period the high priority task hasn't finish its execution of urgent period yet. In the worst case, the low priority task in its urgent period is requested simultaneously with the requests for all higher priority tasks in their urgent periods. If high priority task hasn't finished its execution of urgent period, the low priority task must also haven't finished its execution of urgent period, which is contrary to the precondition that low priority task is running in its normal period. So, in the worst case, the execution in normal period will not be preempted by the execution of high priority task in its urgent period. □ Now, the calculation of maximal DRR in normal period can be presented as follows: Theorem 5. div.head: V. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
div.p: In the section, we evaluate the performance of the NSS algorithm through extensive simulations compared with FTRMFF, ARR2 [12], S-Priority [16] and TPFTRM [10] algorithms. Large task sets with periodic tasks are generated according to the following parameters: As in [12], the performance metric in all the experiments is the ratio N U , where N is the number of processors used by an algorithm to schedule both primary and backup copies and U the summary of all the loads of the primary copies. The ratio reflects the required processor density and can also be regard as the reciprocal of average processor utility. So, the lower the ratio, the better the performance. For any scheduling algorithm, varying L and α , each experiment is repeated 30 times and the average result is calculated. The outcome of the experiments is given in Figure 4, 5 and 6 for the three values of α . It is noted that NSS gains the best performance in the four algorithms for different α . Moreover, by observing Figure 4, when α =0.2, NSS is better than TPFTRM algorithms, whose time complexity are higher for S Priority method. Also, from the three Figures, we can observe that the performance-improving of NSS become decreased with the increase of α compared with ARR2 algorithm. There are two reasons for it: On the one hand, ARR strategy has considered the WCRT in the case of failure when it computes the maximal phasing delay of active backup copy. Hence, it is hard for NSS strategy to deeply improve the schedulability on the active backup copy; On the other hand, ARR strategy has no effect on passive backup copy and NSS can effectively shorten its WCRT in the urgent period, which usually is the scheduling bottom for passive backup copy. So, NSS is more suitable for the low-load periodic task set.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: ARR strategy effectively improves the scheduling performance over the traditional FTRMFF algorithm by applying phasing delay technique to active backup copy. On the basis of the idea of delaying, the NSS strategy presented by the paper postpones the ready time of normal instance task to further improve the schedulability of the task in urgent period in the case of failure. NSS strategy essentially achieves slack stealing to improve the processor utilities and scheduling performance. The experimental results show that NSS is better than ARR, which is the best one in the classic traditional scheduling, under the three different task loads. Especially, when 0.2 α = , the performance increases by up to 15.23% (with an average of 13.6%).

Future studies in this emerging field include two points. First, we will extend the algorithm to schedule more types of tasks, for example aperiodic and sporadic tasks. Second, we will develop an advanced version of NSS which takes task precedence constraints into account.
